analysis.one_liner: Bans unwanted robocalls, lets consumers revoke consent, and requires phone companies to verify caller ID.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Commerce Committee after its June 2018 referral and expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Senator Markey's bill would have rewritten the nation's robocall law to ban robocalls outright — both recorded-voice calls and calls dialed by machine — instead of only restricting certain autodialed calls. It would have let consumers revoke permission to be called at any time and in any reasonable way, created a nationwide database of reassigned phone numbers, extended the deadline to sue over illegal robocalls to four years, and required phone companies to verify that caller ID information is accurate at no extra charge to customers. It also directed the FCC to report to Congress yearly on its robocall enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with a phone. The bill would have banned robocalls rather than merely restricting them [S2][S3], let people revoke consent to be called in any reasonable manner at any time [S2][S3], required the FCC to attach real limits and opt-out rights to the categories of robocalls it has exempted (such as certain informational calls) [S3], and created a reassigned-number database so that people who inherit a phone number stop getting calls meant for the previous owner, with a safe harbor for callers who check the database in good faith [S2][S3]. It would have extended the time limit for suing over robocall violations to four years [S2], required phone companies to implement caller ID authentication technology and barred them from charging subscribers extra for it [S3], and required annual FCC reports to Congress on complaints, penalties, and recommendations for cutting illegal calls by half [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Expands the ban on automated calls to cover all robocalls — calls made by equipment that dials stored or generated numbers and calls using artificial or prerecorded voices — narrowing the exception to equipment that truly needs substantial human intervention for each call.
Lets consumers revoke prior consent to be called at any time and in any reasonable manner, no matter how they originally agreed to be called.

Requires the FCC to add real conditions to its exemptions from the robocall ban — limiting who may call, who may be called, why, how often — and requiring an easy opt-out so people can make exempted callers stop.

Creates a nationwide database of reassigned phone numbers so callers can avoid dialing numbers that now belong to someone else, with a safe harbor for callers who check it in good faith; this protects both the new owner of a number and legitimate callers.

Requires phone companies to implement caller ID authentication technology that verifies where calls really come from and blocks unverified calls, and prohibits them from charging subscribers anything extra for it — a direct hit on spoofing and scam calls.

Extends the statute of limitations for robocall violations to four years and requires annual FCC reports to Congress detailing complaints, penalties, and recommendations for cutting illegal calls by half.

analysis.who_pays: The telemarketing and robocall industry, whose business model the bill would have restricted: the robocall ban would have covered calls that are currently legal, consent could be revoked easily, and callers would have faced a longer window for lawsuits. Debt collectors and other businesses that rely on automated calling would have lost reach. Voice service providers, including wireless carriers and VoIP companies, would have had to report number reassignments to the new database and implement caller ID authentication technology at their own expense, since the bill barred passing the cost to subscribers — though they would also have gained a safe harbor from liability when they checked the reassigned-number database in good faith.
analysis.who_pays_short: Telemarketers, debt collectors, and phone companies

drawbacks.text: The safe harbor for callers who query the reassigned-number database would shift liability away from callers — a caller who checks the database in good faith would not be liable even if the number had in fact been reassigned, which could leave some consumers with fewer remedies when they get calls meant for a previous subscriber.

The carve-out for equipment that 'requires substantial additional human intervention' preserves a gray zone: dialing technology keeps evolving, and deciding what counts as human intervention would likely be litigated, recreating the same definitional fights the bill was meant to settle.

Phone companies would have to build and run caller ID authentication and database reporting at their own expense; the bill blocks them from billing subscribers directly for it, so the costs could surface indirectly in rates.

A broad robocall ban would also sweep in useful automated calls — school alerts, pharmacy reminders, fraud warnings — unless the FCC carefully conditions its exemptions; the bill keeps those exemptions but leaves the line-drawing to the FCC.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefits are large and concrete — fewer scam and telemarketing calls, verified caller ID, an easy way to revoke consent, and a longer window to sue — while the costs fall mainly on an industry built around automated calling and on phone companies' compliance budgets. The main design trade-offs are the caller-side safe harbor and the continued existence of FCC exemptions, both of which temper but do not undo the protections. On balance the benefits to ordinary phone users clearly outweigh the costs, though the bill would have needed careful FCC implementation to avoid blocking legitimate informational calls.

outcome.mechanism: Markey introduced it on June 18, 2018, the Senate sent it to the Commerce Committee, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Markey introduced the Stopping Bad Robocalls Act in the Senate on June 18, 2018.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation — the only action it ever received.
No senator cosponsored the bill, and the Commerce Committee never held a markup or reported it, so it never reached the Senate floor.
The bill expired on January 3, 2019, when the 115th Congress ended; bills not passed by both chambers die at the end of a Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Robocallers, telemarketing operations, and the businesses that rely on automated calling — the restrictions they would have faced were never enacted. Phone companies also avoided the compliance costs of the reassigned-number database and caller ID authentication mandate.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only supporter in the Senate; no colleague cosponsored it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 18, 2018 and took no further action — no markup, no vote, no report to the floor.

against.name: Sen. John Thune
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee that held the bill, never brought it to a markup or committee vote during the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held and no other senator signed on, so the bill never drew enough support to reveal a partisan split beyond its single Democratic sponsor.

industries.note: The bill would have banned robocalls outright rather than merely restricting them, let consumers revoke consent in any reasonable manner, and doubled the window for lawsuits to four years. Its death left the existing, narrower rules in place.

industries.industry: Debt collection and other businesses that rely on automated calling
industries.note: These callers depend on dialing stored lists of numbers; the bill's expanded ban, easy consent revocation, and limits on exempted-call volume would have sharply reduced how many consumers they could reach by machine.

Providers would have had to report number reassignments to a new database and implement caller ID authentication technology without charging subscribers for it, but they also gained a safe harbor from liability when they checked the database in good faith. Blocking spoofed calls helps providers fight fraud on their networks even as compliance costs weigh on them.
